Open on common ground. Most of this room either uses these or is evaluating
them. ellmer is the base — talk to any provider, get structured output. The
other four build on it: shinychat for a chat UI, btw to feed the model your R
context, ragnar for retrieval, vitals for evaluation. These are good starting
points; I'm not here to replace them. The point I want to plant: every one of
these still runs on a prompt you wrote and tuned by hand. That hand-tuning is
the gap dsprrr fills. Keep this slide short — it's the on-ramp.
:::

# The trouble with hand-tuning {.section-divider background-color="#1b2f44"}

## How we build an LLM feature today

- Write a prompt. Run a few inputs. Eyeball the outputs. Tweak the wording. Repeat.
- It breaks when you switch models, or the provider ships a new version
- No held-out test set, so you grade on the examples you happened to look at
- You can't say what you changed, or why it helped

. . .

[Eyeballing a few outputs isn't a measurement you can defend.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
Name the workflow honestly, because everyone in the room has lived it. The
costs are real: prompts are fragile across models, you grade on the examples
you happened to look at, and there's no record of what you changed. For a
regulated audience the last two bullets sting the most — no held-out
evaluation and no audit trail. Land on the line: "seems to work" is not a
metric. That's the hinge into the next slide.
:::

## You already know this workflow

It's just modeling. R users do it every day.

```{=html}
<div class="dgm">
  <div class="dgm-flow">
    <div class="dgm-node is-blue"><span class="k">DECLARE</span><span class="t">a model</span><span class="s">inputs → output</span></div>
    <div class="dgm-arr"><span class="lab">fit</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
    <div class="dgm-node"><span class="k">FIT</span><span class="t">to data</span></div>
    <div class="dgm-arr green"><span class="lab">score</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
    <div class="dgm-node is-green"><span class="k">EVALUATE</span><span class="t">on held-out data</span></div>
    <div class="dgm-arr"><span class="lab">choose</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
    <div class="dgm-node is-orange"><span class="k">COMPARE</span><span class="t">with a metric</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

. . .

[dsprrr runs the same loop on the prompt. You fit it to data, like any other model.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
This is the reframe that makes everything else feel familiar. You declare a
model, fit it to data, evaluate on held-out data, and compare candidates with
a metric. That's how this room already works — clinical models, ML models, all
of it. dsprrr applies the same discipline to the prompt. Nothing here is a new
mindset; it's the mindset you already trust, pointed at a new object.
:::

# What dsprrr adds {.section-divider background-color="#1b2f44"}

## Three pieces, on top of ellmer

dsprrr ports the **DSPy** idea (Stanford NLP) to R.

:::: {.cardgrid}
::: {.gcard}
[01]{.gnum}[Signature]{.gtitle}[Typed inputs and an output. The interface for the task.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard data-accent="green"}
[02]{.gnum}[Module]{.gtitle}[A reusable program: predict, reason, retrieve, or act.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard data-accent="orange"}
[03]{.gnum}[Optimizer]{.gtitle}[Improve the prompt with data and a metric.]{.gbody}
:::
::::

. . .

[Signatures, modules, and optimizers, all built on ellmer.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
Credit the lineage in one line: this is DSPy's idea, ported to R. Three pieces.
A signature declares the contract. A module is the reusable program behind it —
and there's a zoo of them. An optimizer improves the prompt from data. And it's
all on ellmer, so you keep every provider and structured-output feature you
already have. Don't dwell; the next three slides make each piece concrete.
:::

## Signature — declare the contract

```r
library(dsprrr)
library(ellmer)   # the LLM layer dsprrr builds on

# inputs -> a typed output. No prompt text yet.
triage <- signature(
  "ticket -> urgency: enum('urgent', 'normal', 'low')"
)
```

- The signature is the **interface**: typed, immutable.
- The prompt lives *behind* it — swap or optimize it without touching the contract.

. . .

[Declare the interface once; optimize the prompt behind it.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
A signature is a typed input-to-output contract written in one line. Here a
ticket goes in, and a constrained enum comes out — the model cannot return
anything off-menu. Notice there's no prompt here. That separation is the whole
point: the interface is stable, the prompt is a parameter you get to optimize.
This is the same instinct as separating a model's formula from its fitted
coefficients.
:::

## Module — a reusable, optimizable unit

```r
clf <- module(triage, type = "predict")

run(clf, ticket = "I can't log in at all.", .llm = chat_openai())
#> "urgent"
```

A module wraps a signature with a strategy — same signature, different reasoning. The first four are `module(type = ...)`; RAG has its own constructor:

:::: {.cardgrid}
::: {.gcard}
[ ]{.gnum}[predict]{.gtitle}[Direct structured prediction.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard}
[ ]{.gnum}[chain_of_thought]{.gtitle}[Reason step by step first.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard}
[ ]{.gnum}[react]{.gtitle}[Call tools in a loop.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard}
[ ]{.gnum}[program_of_thought]{.gtitle}[Generate and run R code.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard data-accent="green"}
[ ]{.gnum}[rag_module()]{.gtitle}[Retrieve, then answer — with ragnar.]{.gbody}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
A module pairs the signature with a strategy. The simplest is predict —
structured prediction. But the same signature can be wrapped in chain-of-thought
for reasoning, ReAct for tool use, program-of-thought to write and run R, or RAG
to retrieve first. The strategy is swappable; the contract doesn't change. For
today we stay with predict, because the interesting part isn't the strategy —
it's how we improve the prompt.
:::

# Optimize with data {.section-divider background-color="#1b2f44"}

## To improve it with data, you need two things

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**A metric** — what "good" means, as code

```r
metric <- metric_with_feedback(
  function(pred, expected) {
    ok <- tolower(pred) ==
          tolower(expected$urgency)
    list(
      score = as.numeric(ok),
      # feedback carries the *why* — GEPA reflects on it
      feedback = if (ok) "Correct."
        else paste0("Expected '", expected$urgency,
                    "': urgency follows impact, not tone.")
    )
  },
  field = "urgency"
)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Labeled examples** — the data

```r
trainset <- dsp_trainset(
  ticket = c(
    "I can't log in at all.",
    "Typo on your pricing page!!!",
    "How do I export to CSV?"
  ),
  urgency = c("urgent", "low", "normal")
)
```
:::
:::

[The metric defines what "good" means. The examples carry the convention.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
Optimization needs two inputs. First, a metric: a function that says what good
means. With metric_with_feedback it can also return a sentence explaining a
failure — keep that in mind, it matters in two slides. Second, labeled
examples: dsp_trainset is just a data frame of inputs and the right answers.
Notice the examples encode a convention — urgency by usability, not tone — that
a generic prompt won't guess. Writing down what "good" means is the work, and
it's work this audience already does for every analysis.
:::

## Compile the prompt against your data

```r
# mutation_rate = 1, crossover_rate = 0 -> each candidate is a single
# reflective rewrite (full config in talk/scripts/gepa-demo.R)
tp <- GEPA(metric = metric, generations = 4L,
           mutation_rate = 1, crossover_rate = 0, seed = 42)

optimized <- compile(tp, clf, trainset, .llm = chat_openai())
```

```{=html}
<div class="dgm">
  <div class="dgm-flow">
    <div class="dgm-node is-blue"><span class="k">PROMPT</span><span class="t">current instruction</span></div>
    <div class="dgm-arr green"><span class="lab">evaluate</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
    <div class="dgm-node"><span class="k">FAILURES</span><span class="t">what it got wrong</span></div>
    <div class="dgm-arr"><span class="lab">reflect</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
    <div class="dgm-node is-orange"><span class="k">REWRITE</span><span class="t">a better instruction</span><span class="s">repeat</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

::: {.note-orange}
GEPA here is "GEPA-lite": reflective instruction evolution, a faithful but simplified take on the paper (Agrawal et al., 2025).
:::

::: {.notes}
GEPA is the optimizer. It evaluates the current prompt, collects the examples it
got wrong along with the metric's feedback, and asks the model to reflect on why
they failed — then rewrites the instruction. It repeats that over a few
generations, keeping the best. You stop editing the prompt; the metric's feedback
on the failed cases drives the rewrite. Be honest on the footnote — this is a
simplified GEPA, and the package documents exactly how. Then: let's see what it
actually wrote.
:::

## The prompt GEPA wrote {.what-wrote}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Before** — hand-written

::: {.note-blue}
"Classify how urgent this support ticket is: urgent, normal, or low."
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**After** — GEPA, from the failures

::: {.note-green}
"Evaluate the support ticket and classify its urgency as 'urgent', 'normal', or 'low'. Use **'urgent'** for issues that completely block functionality, **'normal'** for issues that hinder usability but allow workarounds or are how-to questions, and **'low'** for minor suggestions or non-critical feedback. Consider the overall impact on user experience when making your classification."
:::
:::
:::

. . .

[I didn't write the prompt on the right. GEPA did, from the cases it got wrong.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
This is the slide to slow down on. On the left is the prompt I wrote — vague, no
rubric. On the right is what GEPA produced after reflecting on the training
failures. Read the right one out loud: it has learned the convention from the
data — that urgency is about whether the product works, not how angry the
customer sounds — without me ever stating it. Nobody typed that prompt; GEPA
derived the rubric from the training labels.
:::

## Did it actually get better? {.score-slide}

```{=html}
<div class="scoreboard">
  <div class="scorebox before"><div class="lbl">Before · hand-written</div><div class="val">67%</div><div class="sub">4 / 6 on held-out test</div></div>
  <div class="scorearrow">→</div>
  <div class="scorebox after"><div class="lbl">After · GEPA-compiled</div><div class="val">83%</div><div class="sub">5 / 6 on held-out test</div></div>
</div>
```

| held-out ticket (tone vs. usability) | truth | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| "…I literally cannot log in right now" | urgent | urgent ✓ | urgent ✓ |
| "Disgraceful!! the homepage image is blurry!!!" | low | low ✓ | low ✓ |
| "sluggish today, but I still got my work done" | normal | low ✗ | **normal ✓** |
| "no big deal… dashboards all error out" | urgent | normal ✗ | normal ✗ |
| "keyboard shortcuts would be nice someday" | low | low ✓ | low ✓ |
| "I can't complete any payments" | urgent | urgent ✓ | urgent ✓ |

::: {style="color:#455468; margin-top:.6rem; font-size:.8em;"}
Real run · gpt-4o-mini · same examples, same metric · `talk/scripts/gepa-demo.R`
:::

::: {.notes}
Same model, same held-out tickets, same metric — the only thing that changed is
the prompt, and the prompt changed itself. Walk the table: every row is a
tone/usability conflict. The flip is the "sluggish but I got my work done" row —
baseline panicked and called it low/urgent by feel; the compiled prompt grades by
the rubric and calls it normal. Be honest about the last miss: "no big deal…
dashboards all error out" is still wrong — a real outage written in a calm voice,
genuinely hard. That's the point: this is measurable, reproducible improvement,
not magic. Real numbers from the script in the repo, not a mock-up.
:::

## GEPA is one of many

:::: {.cardgrid}
::: {.gcard}
[01]{.gnum}[LabeledFewShot]{.gtitle}[Add k labeled demos to the prompt.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard}
[02]{.gnum}[BootstrapFewShot]{.gtitle}[Harvest demos from runs that passed.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard}
[03]{.gnum}[MIPROv2]{.gtitle}[Bayesian search over instructions + demos.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard}
[04]{.gnum}[COPRO]{.gtitle}[Coordinate ascent on instructions.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard}
[05]{.gnum}[KNNFewShot]{.gtitle}[Pick demos by similarity to the input.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard data-accent="orange"}
[06]{.gnum}[GEPA]{.gtitle}[Reflective instruction evolution.]{.gbody}
:::
::::

. . .

[Pick an optimizer like you'd pick a tuning strategy.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
GEPA is one choice. LabeledFewShot just adds demos; BootstrapFewShot harvests
demos from runs that actually passed; MIPROv2 searches instructions and demos
jointly; COPRO and GEPA evolve the instructions; KNNFewShot picks demos by
similarity. Same interface, different search strategy — exactly like choosing
between grid search, random search, or Bayesian tuning. Honesty note: GEPA here
is simplified relative to the paper, and that's documented in the package, not
hidden.
:::

# Inspecting and reproducing {.section-divider background-color="#1b2f44"}

## Every call is traced

```r
inspect_history(n = 1)        # the exact prompt + response
get_last_trace()              # inputs, output, tokens, cost
export_traces(clf)            # a tidy tibble for audit / analysis
```

- The exact prompt the model saw, captured at the time of the call.
- Tokens and cost per call, in a record you can hand to a reviewer.

. . .

[The prompt is just a tibble you can read.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
Optimization is only trustworthy if you can see what happened. Every call is
traced: the exact prompt sent, the response, the inputs, the token counts, the
cost. inspect_history shows it interactively; export_traces hands you a tidy
tibble. For a regulated workflow that's the difference between "the model said
so" and an inspectable record. The prompt isn't a black box — it's data.
:::

## Reproducible and portable

The compiled prompt and demos are just data. Pin them; restore them.

```r
board <- pins::board_folder("pins")
pin_module_config(board, "triage", optimized)   # save the compiled config

config <- pins::pin_read(board, "triage")
clf    <- restore_module_config(config)          # ready to run — no re-optimization
```

- Caching (memory + disk): the same input doesn't cost tokens twice.
- Switch models by re-compiling against your data.

. . .

[When the model changes, you re-fit against the same data.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
A compiled module is just data — the instruction, the demos, the config. Pin it
to a board (local folder, S3, Posit Connect) and restore it in another session
with no re-optimization. Caching means repeated inputs don't re-spend tokens,
which also makes results reproducible. And when a provider ships a new model,
you don't rewrite prompts by hand — you re-run compile against your data. The
maintenance story is "re-fit," not "start over."
:::

## Hand off to vitals {.vitals-handoff}

```r
# the same module becomes a vitals solver
solver <- as_vitals_solver(clf, .llm = chat_openai())

# or bring a vitals scorer back in as a dsprrr metric
m <- as_dsprrr_metric(vitals_scorer)
```

```{=html}
<div class="dgm">

    <div class="dgm-node is-green"><span class="k">DSPRRR</span><span class="t">your module</span></div>
    <div class="dgm-arr"><span class="lab">as_vitals_solver()</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
    <div class="dgm-node is-blue"><span class="k">VITALS</span><span class="t">Task + scorers</span></div>
    <div class="dgm-arr green"><span class="lab">writes</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
    <div class="dgm-node"><span class="k">LOG</span><span class="t">Inspect log viewer</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

[Optimize in dsprrr, evaluate in vitals. The same module does both.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
Close the loop back to the first slide. vitals was one of the five hexes. Your
dsprrr module converts straight into a vitals solver, so the eval framework your
team already trusts scores the thing you just optimized — and writes logs the
Inspect viewer can open. It goes both ways: a vitals scorer can come back in as
a dsprrr metric. The packages are designed to compose, not compete.
:::

# When & why {.section-divider background-color="#1b2f44"}

## Reach for dsprrr when…

:::: {.cardgrid}
::: {.gcard}
[01]{.gnum}[You have labels + a metric]{.gtitle}[Classification, extraction, QA — anything you can score.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard}
[02]{.gnum}[The convention is in the data]{.gtitle}[A rule your examples follow, but you'd struggle to state.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard}
[03]{.gnum}[Multi-step pipelines]{.gtitle}[RAG, or reason → act, that you want to optimize together.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard data-accent="green"}
[04]{.gnum}[Requirements change]{.gtitle}[Re-compile against new data instead of re-writing prompts.]{.gbody}
:::
::: {.gcard data-accent="orange"}
[05]{.gnum}[It has to be reviewable]{.gtitle}[Production work that needs evaluation and an audit trail.]{.gbody}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The "when" the room came for. Reach for dsprrr when you can score the task and
you have labels — classification, extraction, QA. Especially when the
convention lives in the data, not your head, like the urgency rubric. When you
have multi-step pipelines worth optimizing as a whole. When requirements drift
and you'd rather re-fit than re-write. And when the work has to survive review —
evaluation plus traces. If several of these are true, the up-front cost of
writing a metric and labeling examples is worth it.
:::

## Don't reach for it when…

::: {style="border-left:5px solid #ff7518; padding-left:1.1rem; font-size:1.05em;"}
- A **one-off prompt** that won't change → just use ellmer
- **Early exploration**, before you understand the task
- **No labels and no metric** → nothing to optimize against
- It **already works well enough** → not worth the overhead
:::

. . .

[Start by writing down what "good" means. The optimization comes after.]{.takeaway}

::: {.notes}
Be equally clear about when not to. A one-off prompt that won't change doesn't
need any of this — use ellmer directly. Early exploration is for learning the
task by hand; optimize later. With no labels and no metric there's nothing to
optimize against, and if the baseline already works perfectly the ROI is zero.
The honest entry point isn't "install dsprrr" — it's "write down what good
means." Once you've done that, the rest follows.
:::

## Where dsprrr fits

```{=html}
<div class="dgm dgm-fan">
  <div class="dgm-fan__src">
    <div class="dgm-flow">
      <div class="dgm-node is-green"><span class="k">ELLMER</span><span class="t">talk to the model</span></div>
      <div class="dgm-arr"><span class="lab">optimize</span><span class="ln"></span></div>
      <div class="dgm-node is-blue"><span class="k">DSPRRR</span><span class="t">compile the prompt</span></div>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="dgm-fan__hub"></div>
  <div class="dgm-fan__targets">
    <div class="row"><span class="spur"></span><div class="dgm-node"><span class="k">EVALUATE</span><span class="t">vitals</span></div></div>
    <div class="row"><span class="spur"></span><div class="dgm-node"><span class="k">RETRIEVE</span><span class="t">ragnar</span></div></div>
    <div class="row"><span class="spur"></span><div class="dgm-node"><span class="k">DELIVER</span><span class="t">shinychat · shinymcp</span></div></div>
  </div>
</div>
```

> The same building blocks from slide one, now with a prompt you optimize against data.

::: {.notes}
Tie it together. ellmer talks to the model; dsprrr compiles the prompt on top of
it; vitals evaluates it; ragnar feeds it documents; shinychat and shinymcp
deliver it to people. These aren't competitors — they're the building blocks
from the first slide, and dsprrr is the layer that makes the prompt something
you optimize instead of hand-tune. That's the through-line of this whole
hangout: components you can wire into agent-connected workflows.
:::

# Close {.section-divider background-color="#1b2f44"}

## The loop, one more time

::: {style="color:#39729e; font-weight:700; font-size:1.12em;"}
- Declare the contract with a **signature**
- Make "good" measurable with a **metric** + a few labeled examples
- Have an **optimizer** rewrite the prompt, and trace every call
- **Re-compile** when the model or the data changes
:::

- **Install:** `pak::pak("JamesHWade/dsprrr")` (GitHub; experimental)
- **Docs:** [jameshwade.github.io/dsprrr](https://jameshwade.github.io/dsprrr/)
- **This demo:** `talk/scripts/gepa-demo.R`

. . .

::: {style="color:#ff7518; font-weight:700; font-size:1.25em; margin-top:1rem;"}
A prompt is just another thing you fit to data.
:::

::: {.notes}
Recap the loop one last time: signature, metric plus examples, optimizer, trace,
re-compile. Point them at the install and docs, and at the exact script that
produced today's numbers so they can reproduce it. Then the one line I want them
to leave with: stop hand-tuning, compile your prompts. Hand off to deputy /
shinymcp from here.
:::
